results.title: SimpleSpread: Native, open source Mac spreadsheet | Product Hunt
results.content:
Hi Everyone,  
  
I wanted a spreadsheet on my Mac that opens fast, edits an .xlsx file and saves it back, and does nothing else. Numbers converts everything into its own format. Excel is a subscription and a big install for opening a CSV. Google Sheets wants a browser and an account.  
  
So I built SimpleSpread. It is a native Mac app, written entirely in Swift, and the whole spreadsheet stack is from scratch: the model, the formula engine, the XLSX reader and writer (down to the ZIP layer), CSV and the grid. The only outside library is Sparkle, for updates.  
  
• XLSX is the native format. Open a file from Excel, Numbers or Google Sheets, edit it, save it, send it back. Styles, number formats, formulas with cached values, merged ranges and frozen panes all survive the round trip. [...] SimpleSpread

Matt Sergeant [...] • Notarized, and it updates itself in place.  
  
Upfront about what it is not: no charts, no pivot tables, no conditional formatting, no array formulas, no INDIRECT/OFFSET yet, and no collaboration. Frozen panes and merged cells are kept in the file but not drawn yet. It is Apple Silicon only, macOS 14 or later, and en-US number and date input for now.  
  
It's free, MIT licensed and on GitHub, so read it, fork it, send patches. I'd love to hear which missing feature stops you using it day to day. Find & Replace and Paste Values are next on my list.

results.title: The 9 Best Excel Alternatives and Spreadsheet Software in 2026
results.content:
LibreOffice Calc ons:

 No real-time collaboration or chat

LibreOffice Calc is a basic Excel alternative with all the functionality you'd expect from a native modern spreadsheet app on a budget. It's part of the free and open source LibreOffice productivity suite, which began life as a fork of OpenOffice. It's a great alternative to Google Sheets if you're looking for something that runs natively on your Mac, Windows, or Linux desktop.

In practice, LibreOffice Calc feels like an old version of Excel: you can opt for the previous, standard Excel look or the current, tabbed Excel look. Alternatively, there's a sidebar option or a slim contextual single bar. Either way, you immediately feel the app will be easy to use. [...] If you're a Mac user, you might consider Apple Numbers, mainly because it's free—it comes pre-installed on your Mac when you buy it. Numbers is a capable spreadsheet app with a user-friendly tilt. It offers real-time collaboration, can create beautiful charts and graphs, and comes with enough templates to get you started for most common office tasks. Unlike Excel, Numbers cannot handle huge data sets, and it lacks many of the advanced features of Microsoft's app. There's a definite emphasis on presentation and less on data manipulation. But it makes up for it with a simple user interface and an unbeatable price tag. That said, Google Sheets and Zoho Sheet are also free and offer more spreadsheet functionality, which is why Numbers didn't quite make the list here. [...] You can customize the entire interface to display only the functions you're interested in, and there's a full set of keyboard controls for navigating the app quickly. LibreOffice is very user-friendly, with native support for Excel files and a healthy number of templates to save time.

Just because Calc is free and open source doesn't mean it's light on features. Like Excel and Sheets, Calc offers a relatively robust list of supported functions. And in addition to features like conditional formatting and pivot tables, it has a tool called DataPilot. This allows you to pull in raw data from databases and repurpose it in your own spreadsheets. LibreOffice Calc will handle extensive data sets better than web-based spreadsheet apps, but it still comes up short compared to Excel.
